system_in_brief:
REPORTED. Tufa Labs, 1st place (public) ARC Prize 2026 ARC-AGI-2. Whole page text read (20,365 characters); figures and linked supplements were not in the file.

- Model: one LLM, "Qwen3.8-Flash-Next" with "xhigh reasoning". Parameter count not reported. It is a mixture-of-experts model pruned "from 512 to 307 experts with REAP", served from the "RadixArk FP4 quantization" ("we did not observe noticeable degradation compared to unquantized weights"). Earlier models: Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.8-27B.
- Harness: "a variant of the duck harness we shared for ARC3 milestone 1". "We place Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with xhigh reasoning in a persistent Python REPL environment, with clear system and user prompt instructions on the ARC2 task." Grids are given as NumPy arrays (train_in[i], train_out[i], test_in[i]) and "also shown as multimodal image input". The agent must place two attempts in test_out[i][0] and test_out[i][1].
- Tools: "full-featured Python environment ... numpy, scipy, and networkx"; "REPL is persistent (workspace is not cleared between tool calls)"; "a suite of file tools inspired by what a harness like Claude Code would offer"; an optional check(fn) function; an audit turn; compaction by summary at "~49k tokens".
- Compute and time: Kaggle "12-hour" submission on "4xL4"; "pipeline parallelism 2 and tensor parallelism 2"; "an average ~900 tokens per second over a 12-hour submission". Sweeps were "run on B200s" simulating the Kaggle run. 240 tasks per run ("240 total, to match Kaggle").
- Serving: FP8 KV cache, bf16 recurrent state, MTP speculative decoding drafting 4 tokens with a fine-tuned drafter, custom CPU KV offload cache, own vLLM fork.
- Code is "mostly LLM written"; "We mainly used frontier Anthropic and OpenAI models."

Design principle in their words: "Provide a descriptive, powerful, and flexible harness - and then get out of the LLM's way".
loops:
REPORTED, one entry per iterative element.

1. Agentic REPL loop within a pass. The model writes code, sees the execution result and continues; state persists in the workspace. Fed back: tool output as text, plus code and variables in the persistent REPL. Number of turns: not reported; bounded by context and the time budget. Whether more turns help: not reported directly.

2. check(fn) loop. "The agent can, if it chooses to, write a transform function fn that maps train_in[i] to train_out[i]. It can then call check(fn), which will verify the mapping and provide diagnostics to the agent if it fails." Fed back: diagnostics (text) on its own code. Rounds: not reported. Effect: no significant gain when optional versus off (off: +1.2 ± 1.8), and forcing it hurt (mandatory: −2.6 ± 1.4).

3. Audit turn (self-critique, one round). "Once the agent has submitted an answer, we do an additional 'audit turn'. The agent gets a new prompt, repeating the question and its answers, with a targeted set of audit questions it works through, potentially updating its answer. It's also asked to indicate how confident it is". Fed back: its own answer as text. Rounds: 1. Effect: none measurable (audit off: +0.7 ± 1.4); "We were surprised to see no statistically significant gain from the audit turn, the check function or 10 passes".

4. Compaction by self-written summary (memory across context resets). "When the context runs into its limit (~49k tokens), we ask the agent to write a summary of its work so far. The context is then reset, showing the agent the system prompt, original user prompt, summary, the last tool call, and a resume prompt." Fed back: the model's own summary (text); the REPL workspace and files presumably persist (my inference). Number of compactions per task: not reported. Effect: the self-summary beats mechanical pruning ("prune to half": −4.7 ± 1.4).

5. Multiple independent passes. "We run each task up to 10 times as time allows, each pass starting fresh with no knowledge of the others." Nothing is fed back between passes, so this is resampling, not recursion. A scheduler allocates further passes by disagreement between passes. In practice "about 5% of tasks had finished no pass by the deadline, 32% one, 60% two and under 3% more than two". Effect: saturated; up to 2 instead of up to 10 passes: −0.2 ± 1.3.

6. Drafter fine-tuned on own traces (weights). "We fine-tuned Qwen's built-in MTP head on a combined dataset of ARC2 and ARC3 traces of our agents." This is distillation of the agent's own traces into the speculative-decoding head. It affects speed only: accepted tokens per draft "from 2.09 to 2.36". Rounds: not reported (appears to be a single round).

7. RL training of the model on ARC (weights). Helped earlier Qwen models; "we could not achieve any such gains with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next". Details are deferred to the paper-track submission.

8. Distillation of a stronger model's traces (Kimi K3.1 Pro) into Flash-Next (weights; not self-generated). Hurt accuracy.

Not present or not reported: programs that write programs beyond the transform function; test-time training on the test tasks; notes carried across tasks or across passes ("each pass starting fresh").

INFERRED: every within-task loop that feeds the model its own output back as text for another round (audit, mandatory check, extra passes) is flat or negative for this strong model. The only own-output loop with a clear positive effect is the summary used as memory, and it is compared against a cruder alternative, not against a larger context.
feedback_signals:
REPORTED.

Loops with an external signal:
- REPL loop: Python execution results (real program output).
- check(fn): verification against the given train pairs: it "will verify the mapping and provide diagnostics to the agent if it fails. This provides it a robust way to check its own work." This is the only verifier, and it covers the train examples only; there is no signal on the test output.
- Pass scheduling and selection: agreement between independent passes ("ranked by how many passes returned them first, then by how many returned them second"). This is a consistency signal between samples, not ground truth.
- No environment score is available at test time (the submission gets 2 attempts, and no feedback is described).

Loops closed on the model's own judgement:
- Audit turn: the model re-examines its own answer against "a targeted set of audit questions". No external signal. Measured effect is indistinguishable from zero (off: +0.7 ± 1.4).
- Self-reported confidence: used only as a tie-break. It predicts across tasks but not within a task: "the agent is more confident on tasks it is more likely to get right" but "the agent is not more confident on correct passes than on incorrect passes". "the lack of intra-task prediction makes this of limited value".
- Compaction summary: the model's own summary, with no check of its correctness.

What the write-up says about loops without an external signal: there is no general statement. The specific evidence is the audit null result and the confidence finding above.

Notable in the other direction: making the external check compulsory hurt (−2.6 ± 1.4); "Tools should help the agent, not restrict it."

INFERRED: the self-judgement signal carries information about task difficulty but none about which of the model's own attempts on a task is right. A self-critique loop on a single task therefore has little to select on, which fits the audit null result. The write-up does not draw this connection itself.
sampling_and_temperature:
REPORTED.

- Temperature: the submitted value is not reported. Temperature and reasoning effort were swept ("sampling settings such as temperature and reasoning effort"), but no per-value results are in the page text.
- Per-phase temperatures: "We tried using different sampling temperatures for reasoning, writing code, and summarizing, but found no benefit."
- Reasoning effort: "xhigh".
- Samples: up to 10 independent passes per task, each "starting fresh". Realised counts in the 12-hour simulation: about 5% of tasks with zero passes, 32% one, 60% two, under 3% more than two. Time, not the cap, is the limit.
- Each pass returns two grids ("two, the second optional"): "this is critical for puzzles with a small ambiguity the agents can't otherwise resolve". One grid per pass: −3.2 ± 1.4.
- Selection with up to two passes: "the first attempt is the first pass's first grid, and the second attempt is the second pass's first grid if it differs, otherwise the next different grid those passes returned."
- Selection with three or more passes: grids "ranked by how many passes returned them first, then by how many returned them second, with the agent's self-reported confidence ... breaking ties. The top two are submitted."
- Priority for extra passes: tasks where passes disagree come first, then tasks with the fewest passes; within a group, the task with the fewest tokens spent, "counting each earlier pass as 150K extra tokens".
- Effect of more samples: capping at 2 instead of 10 passes changes the score by −0.2 ± 1.3, i.e. no measurable gain from more than two.
- Diversity tricks (prompt variation, augmentation, different seeds or temperatures per pass): not reported.
- Using confidence to steer passes to hard tasks: "since those also tend to cost more tokens we weren't able to gain any score this way".

INFERRED: the useful diversity is asking for a second alternative inside one pass, where the model knows the 2-attempt rule, not more independent resampling.
training_and_self_generated_data:
REPORTED.

- The final system uses an essentially untrained base model. Figure caption: "The first untrained Qwen3.8-Flash-Next run scored 71.1%, 12.8 points above our best RL-trained Qwen3.8-27B (58.3%)."
- Reinforcement learning: "We expected reinforcement learning to be the keystone of our submission, and spent the bulk of our time and resources across ARC2 and ARC3 on this. We initially found promising results with earlier Qwen models, including improvements on held-out games/tasks in offline evaluations for both ARC2 and ARC3, and leaderboard improvements on ARC2. However, we could not achieve any such gains with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next." The size of the earlier gains, the RL data and the method are not reported here (deferred to the paper track).
- Self-generated traces: used only for the speculative-decoding drafter: "We fine-tuned Qwen's built-in MTP head on a combined dataset of ARC2 and ARC3 traces of our agents. In real gameplay, fine-tuning increased ARC2's accepted tokens per draft from 2.09 to 2.36." This is a throughput gain, not an accuracy gain.
- Distillation from a stronger teacher: "Distilling Kimi K3.1 Pro into Flash-Next. We found no benefit on ARC2; Kimi uses fewer tokens but does not improve score. The distilled Flash model also ends up more token efficient, but gets significantly more tasks wrong than the baseline Flash model."
- Pruning with fine-tuning: "we also developed techniques to prune further with fine-tuning, but we applied those only to ARC3."
- Test-time training on the test tasks: not reported (none described).
- Synthetic or human-made training data for the final model: not reported.
- "the model checkpoint" was a sweep parameter; results per checkpoint are not in the page text.

INFERRED: for the strongest model, weight updates from ARC-specific data (RL, teacher distillation) gave nothing or made accuracy worse. The one place self-generated traces paid off is a component that only has to predict what the model will say next, not improve it.
ablations_and_numbers:
REPORTED.

Progress figure (caption):
- First untrained Qwen3.8-Flash-Next run: 71.1% public.
- Best RL-trained Qwen3.8-27B: 58.3% (12.8 points lower).
- "Harness upgrades and optimization via sweep on that model then added a further 17 points" (about 88% public; the final public score is not stated as a number in the text).
- "These steps are not controlled comparisons, and repeat submissions of one configuration differ by a few points."

Ablation table. Method: a random combined parameter sweep analysed with "ordinary least-squares and LASSO", not 1:1 ablations. Simulated 12-hour run on 4xL4, 240 tasks ("a mix of the eval tasks and the harder train tasks"), baseline "~89". Values are alternative minus submitted, with 95% CI; negative means the submitted setting is better.

| Parameter | Submitted | Alternative | Score change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passes per task | up to 10 | up to 2 | −0.2 ± 1.3 |
| Grids per pass | two, second optional | one | −3.2 ± 1.4 |
| File tools | on | off | +1.6 ± 1.2 |
| check function | optional | off | +1.2 ± 1.8 |
| check function | optional | mandatory | −2.6 ± 1.4 |
| Grid display | images | images and text | −2.6 ± 1.5 |
| Grid display | images | text | −6.2 ± 1.6 |
| At context limit | summary | prune to half | −4.7 ± 1.4 |
| Audit turn | on | off | +0.7 ± 1.4 |

Authors' reading: "We were surprised to see no statistically significant gain from the audit turn, the check function or 10 passes in this final sweep, and file tools even suggest a slight degradation".

Other numbers:
- Harness comparison on the 120 evaluation puzzles: Qwen Code and an adaptation of ARC Prize's Provider Adapter harness both "score worse than our harness"; the latter shows "very weak performance". The numbers are in a figure that is not in the text: not reported.
- Telegraphic reasoning on Qwen3.8-27B: "~10 points on the leaderboard".
- Drafter fine-tuning: accepted tokens per draft 2.09 to 2.36 (drafting 4).
- Pruning: 512 to 307 experts.
- Throughput: ~900 tokens per second.
- Context limit: ~49k tokens.
- Pass-count distribution: 5% / 32% / 60% / under 3% for zero / one / two / more passes.
- Confidence analysis: 167 tasks (120 eval, 47 selected train).
failures_and_limits:
REPORTED.

Did not work:
- RL on the strong model: "we could not achieve any such gains with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next", after spending "the bulk of our time and resources" on it.
- Telegraphic (concise) reasoning: worked on the 27B model via "prompt injection to force the model into a more concise reasoning mode"; on Flash-Next "we were unable to reliably trigger it".
- Per-phase temperatures: "found no benefit".
- Distilling Kimi K3.1 Pro: "more token efficient, but gets significantly more tasks wrong than the baseline".
- Confidence to guide effort: "we weren't able to gain any score this way"; no intra-task predictive power.
- INT4 KV cache: "we found the drop in quality too high for ARC2".

Features with no measurable benefit in the final sweep: audit turn, check function, 10 passes. File tools "even suggest a slight degradation" (off: +1.6 ± 1.2). The mandatory check, adding text grids to images, text-only grids and pruning the context instead of summarising were all clearly worse.

Weak points the authors name:
- Time budget: "about 5% of tasks had finished no pass by the deadline".
- The sweep "simply didn't have enough resolving power (i.e. needed more runs)" is offered as a possible explanation for the nulls.
- Some decisions "based on earlier harness versions".
- Reasoning excerpts show "where its reasoning still breaks down"; details are in a linked supplement, not reported here.

Never tried: "A 'finish now' prompt when the submission timer is nearly up"; "Scene decomposition techniques such as the segmentation tool our ARC3 submission uses."
general_vs_specific:
REPORTED evidence for the title claim.

1. Model swap beats domain training: the untrained Flash-Next first run scored 71.1% versus 58.3% for the best RL-trained Qwen3.8-27B. RL gains seen on earlier models did not transfer to the stronger one.

2. ARC-specific harness features add little: "Our harness does have several complex ARC2-specific features, but they actually add very little performance." The audit turn, check function and many passes are not significant in the sweep. The ablation section says it shows "that the details don't matter all that much!"

3. Restriction hurts a strong model: the mandatory check costs −2.6. "With weaker models such as Qwen3.8-27B, we found that there is more to be gained from restrictive harnesses that force the model to reason in productive ways. But as model capability increases, it pays off more and more to just get out of the way and let the model do its thing."

4. The same design transfers across tasks: "It is very similar to our ARC3 solution, and indeed many of the top teams' solutions shared at time of writing are based on the same principle." "most content in both writeups is identical - this commonality is actually an important learning."

5. Explicit link to Sutton: "general methods that leverage scale - in our case via the underlying model - ultimately beat methods that build in human domain knowledge."

6. Final thoughts: "we found that we needed general solutions instead: a harness that provides task description and tools and then gets out of the way, a powerful base model, and lots and lots of tokens."

Qualifications in the write-up itself:
- The harness is not irrelevant: "getting some basic properties of the harness right does matter a lot". Qwen Code (powerful, but the task is not explained) and the ARC Prize adapter (task explained, no REPL) both score worse. The three properties named are "Descriptive", "Powerful", "Flexible".
- About 17 points still came from "Harness upgrades and optimization via sweep", and much of the score comes from serving engineering.
- "Note that these observations are specifically for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next."

INFERRED: the claim is conditional on model strength. What still matters is general-purpose: a clear task statement, code execution, image input, a good memory strategy and throughput. The 71.1 versus 58.3 comparison confounds model size and generation with training, and the authors say these steps are not controlled.
evaluation_caveats:
REPORTED.

- This is the public leaderboard only: "1st place (public)". Private scores are not reported. The final public score is not stated as a number in the text (71.1 plus "a further 17 points" is implied).
- Run-to-run variance: "repeat submissions of one configuration differ by a few points". Progress steps "are not controlled comparisons".
- Ablations are regression estimates from a random multi-parameter sweep (OLS and LASSO), "not simple 1:1 ablations; these are too expensive", and choosing values "may also involve subjective judgment". Several CIs include zero; the authors admit possibly insufficient "resolving power".
- The ablation set is the public eval tasks plus "the harder train tasks" (240), simulated on B200s, not actual Kaggle runs. Baseline "~89" is on that chosen set, not the leaderboard.
- Harness comparison only "over the 120 evaluation puzzles"; numbers are in a figure.
- Findings are stated to be specific to Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.
- Possible contamination or overfitting of the base model to ARC is not addressed by the authors. A commenter (49th place) writes: "it is no suprise to assume that both the qwen models were hill climbed of some sort on arc agi 2 tasks." This is a commenter's speculation, not evidence.
- The harness and parameters were tuned by sweep on public eval and train tasks, so there is some risk of fitting to the public set; the authors do not discuss it. (INFERRED)
- Supplementary material is "mainly AI written with human review"; the linked supplements, figures and the paper-track details were not part of the file read.
other_notable:
REPORTED.

- The self-confidence result is the most directly relevant finding for self-reinforcing loops. Citing Kadavath et al., the authors test whether stated confidence predicts correctness. Across tasks: "There is clear correlation". Within a task: "no, the agent is not more confident on correct passes than on incorrect passes." The model's self-assessment tracks task difficulty, not the correctness of a particular attempt.
- The self-written summary as memory beats mechanical context pruning (−4.7 ± 1.4 for "prune to half"): a positive case of the model's own compressed output being fed back.
- Images alone beat images plus text (−2.6) and text only (−6.2): adding a redundant representation hurt.
- Telling the model the real problem statement (2 attempts) and letting it produce both alternatives itself beats getting the alternatives from independent passes: "this tells the agent the actual problem statement".
- Capability dependence of scaffolding: weaker models gain from "restrictive harnesses that force the model to reason in productive ways"; stronger models are harmed by them.
- Cost accounting: every feature is evaluated inside a full simulated time-limited run, "so that a choice's throughput cost counts against its score". An extra loop round must pay for the tokens it consumes; some nulls (audit, passes) may partly reflect that trade-off rather than zero per-token value. (The last clause is my inference.)
- A concise reasoning mode forced by prompt injection gave "~10 points" on the 27B model but could not be reliably triggered on the stronger model.
- Distillation made the model more token-efficient but less accurate, i.e. shorter reasoning traded against correctness.

INFERRED patterns for an experiment on self-reinforcing loops:
1. Loops grounded in execution are kept; loops grounded only in self-judgement show no gain.
2. Returns to extra rounds or samples saturate very early (about 2).
3. Forced self-verification can be net negative.
4. Benefits of loop scaffolding shrink or reverse as base-model capability rises.

All four rest on a single team's sweep with CIs of about ±1.3 to 1.8 points and on one model.

system_in_brief:
Source: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-DSSE/85db304a-b0fa-5d03-b685-f9acf8fac842/scratchpad/kaggle_arc/agi3.json (27,240 characters of page text, read in full; figures are not in the text, only their captions). Tufa Labs, 2nd place public, ARC-AGI-3, write-up dated Nov 9, 2026.

REPORTED
- Task: "an interactive turn-based multi-level game, with a 64x64 grid updating after each action"; "beating levels in fewer actions scores higher".
- Model: one LLM, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next "with xhigh reasoning". Parameter count is not reported. It is a mixture-of-experts model served in "FP4 expert weights" (RadixArk FP4 quantization) and pruned "from 512 to 307 experts with REAP, and from 307 to 205 with distillation" ("108–268 per layer"). Earlier models used: Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.8-27B (a 9B model is mentioned in a comment).
- Harness: the 'seal', "a variant of the duck harness we shared for milestone 1". "We place Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with xhigh reasoning in a persistent Python REPL environment, with clear system and user prompt instructions on the ARC3 task." Moves go through a `submit_action` function; "it can batch multiple moves inside one function call". "The agent is never told about or allowed to use the UNDO action."
- Inputs to the agent: "User prompts showing the gameplay grid as multimodal image input, along with descriptions of moves that were done and Python visual summaries" plus "A history object in the REPL, containing among others gameplay and animation frames as NumPy arrays."
- Tools: numpy, scipy, networkx; "a suite of file tools inspired by what a harness like Claude Code would offer"; `segment()`; `describe_animation()`; automatic frame-delta descriptions as verified Python (built with "a minimum description length (MDL) approach"); optional `world_model.py` with `initial_state()`, `do_move(state, move)`, `render(state)`, `test_world_model()`, and "an automatic breadth-first search (BFS)".
- Compute and time: Kaggle submission of 9 hours on an RTX PRO 6000 ("simulates the 9-hour Kaggle submission on an RTX PRO 6000"); offline sweeps "run on B200s". "Altogether we generate an average ~3200 tokens per second over a 9-hour submission." "Up to 80 games decode at once"; "There is no per-level token cap on Kaggle; engine slots go to the games that have spent the fewest tokens so far, so the games share the 9 hours evenly." Context limit "~148k tokens".
- Serving: INT4 KV cache, bf16 recurrent state, MTP speculative decoding "drafting 3 tokens", custom kernels, CPU KV offload cache.
- Score: "our best score rose from 18.8% to 70.2% by the code deadline" on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (public leaderboard).

INFERRED
- ~3200 tokens/s over 9 h is roughly 100 million generated tokens per submission (my arithmetic, not stated).
loops:
REPORTED (each item: what is fed back / form / rounds / trend)

1. Act-observe loop in a persistent REPL. The agent writes Python, submits moves, and gets the new frame back as image, text and NumPy history. "The REPL is persistent; the workspace is not cleared between tool calls or moves; it is, however, reset between levels." Form: code state plus conversation text. Rounds: unbounded within the 9-hour shared clock; number of turns per game not reported.

2. Files as cross-level memory. "Files are not reset between levels." Form: files written by the agent. Whether more carried-over notes help: not reported separately (only the joint ablation "none, and no file tools −4.2 ± 2.0" versus "none" −2.7 ± 2.1 for the world model).

3. Compaction / self-summary. "When the context runs into its limit (~148k tokens), we ask the agent to write a summary of its work so far. The context is then reset, showing the agent the system prompt, original user prompt, summary, the last tool call, and a resume prompt." Form: text written by the model, re-read by the model. Rounds: as often as the limit is hit; count not reported. Effect: not ablated in ARC3 ("due to code limitations, we did not ablate the compaction scheme"); in ARC2 "our submitted summarization scheme gained 4.7 ± 1.4 points over the simple pruning scheme of the original duck". Whether repeated summaries of summaries degrade: not reported.

4. End-of-level reflection. "When the agent beats a level, it is presented with the level's final frame and invited to reflect on what it has learned." Form: text. Once per cleared level. Ablation: off = −0.9 ± 1.5 (interval includes zero).

5. Strategy audit when stuck. "A similar invitation to reflect ... is sent if it is stuck on the same level for a very long time (specifically if a level has taken 300,000 tokens without being cleared)." Form: text, self-critique. Ablation: off = −0.1 ± 1.6 (no measurable effect).

6. World-model loop (model writes a program, the program is tested against history, then used to search). The agent "can optionally write a formal single-level Python world model in world_model.py"; `test_world_model()` "to verify its world model describes history correctly"; "Whenever a move done through submit_action leads to a mispredicted board, the move sequence stops immediately"; with a working model "an automatic breadth-first search (BFS) searches for winning or unknown states". Form: code. Rounds: revise until history is reproduced; number not reported. Usage: "the agent chooses to use this world model on about half of the games it plays, and may switch within a game." Trend: optional beats both mandatory (−3.5 ± 2.0) and none (−2.7 ± 2.1).

7. Prompted assumption re-check: "If your reasoning concludes that a level is impossible, one of your assumptions about the rules is wrong: list the assumptions that conclusion rests on and test the ones you have not directly observed". Form: text instruction pointing to tests in the game. Effect: not reported.

8. Training on its own traces (weights): the speculative-decoding draft head was fine-tuned "on a combined dataset of ARC2 and ARC3 traces of our agents"; accepted tokens per draft "from 1.81 to 2.00". This changes speed, not what the main model outputs (speculative decoding verifies drafts).

9. Reinforcement learning on the model (weights): worked on earlier Qwen models, "we could not achieve any such gains with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next".

10. Distillation from another model's outputs (Kimi K3.1 Pro into Flash-Next): no benefit, more errors (see failures).

Loops considered but not built: "A separate 'reviewer' agent that provides suggestions to the agent actually playing"; "Retrying a level from a checkpoint of the conversation and files when clearly stuck"; "World models that must cover every level played so far"; "Playing the agent's acting code through its world model first, and warning when it leads nowhere useful."

Saturation with more rounds or tokens: not reported as a curve in the text. Only indirect statements: the authors need "lots and lots of tokens", and GPT-6.1 (Sol) "would continue to score higher than the 54.8% shown above - we stopped it due to cost reasons".

INFERRED
- The two loops closed purely on the model's own text (reflection, strategy audit) have the smallest measured effects (−0.9 ± 1.5, −0.1 ± 1.6); the loops tied to execution or to the environment (world model, compaction that keeps the task going, the image input) show the larger ones. The authors do not draw this contrast themselves.
feedback_signals:
REPORTED
- Environment feedback: every action returns a new 64x64 frame (plus animation frames); level completion is observed ("When the agent beats a level..."). The scoring signal is action efficiency ("beating levels in fewer actions scores higher"); the agent is told so in the prompt ("Your goal is to be both token-efficient and action-efficient."). Whether the agent sees a numeric score is not reported.
- Program execution as verifier: `test_world_model()` checks the model's program against recorded history ("this function is flexible, and the agent can configure its strictness"). Misprediction during play is an automatic stop signal: "Whenever a move done through submit_action leads to a mispredicted board, the move sequence stops immediately. This prevents wasted actions."
- Harness-computed, machine-verified descriptions: frame deltas and animations are given as Python whose "assert holds": "The code is exact: it was run against these frames and its assert holds, so there is no need to check it against the pixels." Also "based on visual decomposition, without understanding the game".
- Search over the verified model: BFS "searches for winning or unknown states".
- Loops on the model's own judgement only: compaction summary, end-of-level reflection, strategy audit. The strategy audit is triggered by an external counter (300,000 tokens without clearing the level), but its content is the model's own reflection.
- Statement about loops without an external signal: not reported as such. The closest items are the prompt line that forces untested assumptions back to observation ("test the ones you have not directly observed — above all, anything the game did that your model did not predict") and the ablation numbers for reflection (−0.9 ± 1.5) and strategy audit (−0.1 ± 1.6).
- For RL: "improvements on held-out games/tasks in offline evaluations" with earlier models; reward design is not described here (deferred to the paper-track write-up).

INFERRED
- The design pushes the model's beliefs through an executable check wherever possible; the purely introspective steps are kept but are statistically indistinguishable from zero effect in the sweep.
sampling_and_temperature:
REPORTED
- Temperature value: not reported. Temperature and reasoning effort were among the swept parameters: "sampling settings such as temperature and reasoning effort". Final reasoning effort: "xhigh".
- Phase-specific temperatures failed: "We tried using different sampling temperatures for reasoning, writing code, and summarizing, but found no benefit."
- Number of samples, voting, selection among candidates: not reported. Each game is played once by one agent; there is no ensemble or majority vote described. (An online game cannot be replayed freely; UNDO is withheld.)
