5. Weight-level self-reinforcement can regress. Reported: "longer single-game GRPO training regressed" on Flash-Next. No mechanism is given.

6. RL is described as repairing specific failure modes (loops, hypothesis fixation), not as adding general reasoning: "Domain-specific post-training does not tackle this general reasoning capability".

7. External context: the authors cite last year's top ARC papers on "tiny recursive networks, evolutionary program synthesis and solving without pretraining" as the paradigm they expected and that was overtaken.

Missing for loop research (not reported): temperatures, number of iterations, any curve of score versus rounds, any stopping rule, any measure of diversity collapse. These would have to come from the ARC2/ARC3 write-ups or the supplement (arc_prize_2026_supplementary.zip), which this file does not contain.

No instructions addressed to the reader were found in the file; it was treated purely as data.

patterns.pattern: Run-to-run variance is as large as most reported effects, and the team ends with results it cannot classify as "no effect" or "not measured well enough".
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: Variance: "These steps are not controlled comparisons, and repeat submissions of one configuration differ by a few points." Results the authors cannot classify: the trained 27B checkpoint "scored 58.3% against 48.6% for our best untrained baseline ... though submission variability leaves the gain uncertain"; RL on the strong model was "inconclusive", with the hedge "Our results do not categorically rule out ARC-specific fine-tuning of larger models"; for the nulls of the final ARC2 sweep (audit turn, check function, 10 passes) they offer that the sweep "simply didn't have enough resolving power (i.e. needed more runs)". Method: effects are regression estimates from a random joint sweep ("ordinary least-squares and LASSO"), "not simple 1:1 ablations; these are too expensive", and final choices "may also involve subjective judgment"; the 95% intervals are ±1.2 to ±2.1 points around effects of 0.1 to 6.2 points. Public versus private: both solution write-ups report public placements and the configuration was tuned on public tasks; for the private evaluation one run had to be picked: "submission ID 57872450 (87.36%; another notebook that scored 88.06% was not selected for private-leaderboard evaluation)". The held-out sets behind the training claims are small (47 puzzles, 43 generated games).
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: All rounds, and most directly the positive control of round 1, which failed narrowly for a statistical reason. This is method, not ARC content, so it carries over without analogy. The write-ups show what it costs to decide after the data what counts as an effect: the team cannot tell whether three of its features do nothing or were measured too coarsely. The experiment's pre-set verdict rules already prevent the worst of this. What rules alone do not supply is power: a gate or a positive control that cannot detect the expected effect at the planned sample size will again return a verdict nobody can use. The public/private split corresponds to the statements used to derive directions versus the held-out statements. Round 2 was designed after round 1 had reported behaviour on the held-out statements, so those statements may already have shaped design choices.
patterns.what_to_do: Before the round-2 GPU run, as numbers written down and not as changes to the frozen plan: (1) From round-1 data, compute the seed-to-seed spread of each gated quantity under identical settings, and from it the smallest effect that each gate and the positive control can detect at the planned numbers of texts and seeds. If the positive control is underpowered again, record that now, not after the run. (2) Confirm that the pre-set rules have three outcomes: effect, no effect (the interval excludes a pre-set smallest effect of interest), and inconclusive. (3) Check whether any round-2 design choice (for example push sizes or the axis definition) drew on round-1 behaviour on the held-out statements; if so, the verdict needs a fresh held-out set, logged before any data. (4) Fix in advance which runs and seeds give the verdict; do not choose among runs afterwards. (5) In the phase diagram of (B) the object is a boundary, that is an interaction of push size and temperature. Do not summarise it by main effects as the write-ups' regression does, and put replicates near the expected boundary where the plan leaves that open.

patterns.pattern: Almost every loop-related effect is conditional on the model: a recipe that works on one model vanishes or reverses on a stronger one.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: Training: RL gave significant held-out gains on Qwen3.8-27B (ARC3 "9.40→22.1%" on 43 training-disjoint games; ARC2 "46.3→51.9% on 47 held-out puzzles") and none on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ("two trained Kaggle submissions (85.3% and 84.3%) matched our untrained runs"); "RL gains vanished on our strongest model"; also "RL gains tended to shrink even with the 27B model as we improved the base harness". A prompt-level mode: on Qwen3.8-27B "prompt injection to force the model into a more concise reasoning mode" gave "~10 points" (ARC2) and "~8 points" (ARC3); on Flash-Next "While we also found evidence of such a mode in Flash-Next, we were unable to reliably trigger it." The mode exists in both models; the handle that reaches it does not carry over. Scaffolding: "With weaker models such as Qwen3.8-27B, we found that there is more to be gained from restrictive harnesses that force the model to reason in productive ways. But as model capability increases, it pays off more and more to just get out of the way". Authors' own scope: "Note that these observations are specifically for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next." Confound: the step from 27B to Flash-Next changes size, generation and architecture at once (mixture of experts, pruned, quantised; "Quantization and expert routing made training harder too"), and the progress steps are, in the authors' words, "not controlled comparisons".
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Two places. (a) Round 2 (A), the toy on whether recipes transfer across models: behaviour-level evidence that an intervention recipe can fail to transfer even between related models, and that a failed recipe does not show that the target lacks the feature (the concise mode is present in Flash-Next but cannot be triggered). This is not evidence about directions; it is a caution for how a failed transfer is read. (b) Scope of every round: Qwen3-1.7B is far below the smallest model named in the write-ups (9B, in an author comment) and, by its name, an earlier version. If loop-related effects change sign with capability there, a result on the 1.7B model, decay or sustain, cannot be extended to larger models in either direction. In the write-ups the small models are the ones with self-reinforcing failures ("looping or refusing to drop an incorrect hypothesis"); by analogy a small model should show more carry of its own earlier text, not less. That last step is a guess.
patterns.what_to_do: (a) In the (A) toy, report two numbers per target model: whether the feature is present in the target (a probe trained in the target) and whether the source model's recipe moves it. If the frozen plan reports only the second, state this as a limit of the verdict and add the first in round 1b. (b) Name the model and the block in every verdict. For round 1b, consider repeating one measurement, the loop gain per round at the round-1 settings, on one larger model of the same family; one number, not a new study.

patterns.pattern: Effects measured under a fixed budget mix the value of a change with its cost; the largest single step in the write-ups came from speed alone.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: ARC3: "the largest single step (+18.0 points) coming from speculative decoding", a change in throughput only. Every feature is judged inside a full simulated run "so that a choice's throughput cost counts against its score"; the comparison with Qwen Code is "at matched generated tokens"; "optimal balance of tokens per second and quality acts as a multiplier for any solution". Steering extra passes to low-confidence tasks failed because "those also tend to cost more tokens".
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Round 2 (B) and (C). The principle is method and needs no analogy: a comparison can be read only when the cost variable is matched. The experiment already matches on damage (KL). The write-ups point to a second cost variable that damage does not cover, quantity. In the loop a larger push or a higher temperature changes how long the texts are, how many are usable and how degenerate they are, and the next direction is a mean whose noise depends on all three. A cell of the phase diagram could then differ from its neighbour in the noise of the read step and not in the loop gain.
patterns.what_to_do: Check in the frozen (B) and (C) plans that the number of texts and of tokens entering each read step is the same in every cell and in the foreign-axis and damage-matched controls, and that degenerate texts are handled by a pre-set rule (kept, or dropped with the count reported). The noise floor has to be estimated per cell at that same count, since it will rise with temperature. If counts cannot be equalised, report them per cell next to the gain.

patterns.pattern: Steps where the model only re-reads and judges its own output show no measurable gain; measurable gains sit in components that are checked against something outside the model. The contrast is the readers' inference, not a claim of the authors, and it has exceptions.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: Self-judgement steps: ARC2 audit turn (the model re-examines its submitted answers against audit questions), switching it off: "+0.7 ± 1.4". ARC3 level reflection off: "−0.9 ± 1.5"; strategy audit off: "−0.1 ± 1.6". Paper: "removing scene segmentation, frame differences, level reflection or the strategy audit each moves the ARC3 score by less than a point, within noise." Authors: "We were surprised to see no statistically significant gain from the audit turn, the check function or 10 passes in this final sweep". Anchored components: a harness "which offers one action per call and no Python tool" scores 0.17% on ARC3 (final submission 70.24%); the optional code world model, tested against recorded history and stopped at the first mispredicted board, against none: "−2.7 ± 2.1"; the prompt sends untested beliefs back to observation ("list the assumptions that conclusion rests on and test the ones you have not directly observed"). The only loop with a gain shown on held-out material is RL with the game score as reward on the weaker model (see P8). Exceptions and confounds: (1) check(fn), which tests the model's transform on the given train pairs, is an external check and is also null (off: "+1.2 ± 1.8"), as are the machine-verified frame descriptions ("−0.7 ± 1.6"). (2) A self-written summary with no check on it helps (see P7). (3) The 0.17% case changes harness, action batching and Python tool together. (4) Features are scored under a fixed time budget, so a null means no net gain per unit of compute. (5) The reflection steps were tested on top of an agent that already has execution feedback; they measure marginal value, not a loop with self-judgement alone. (6) Low power, by the authors' own account.
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Round 1 interpretation. At the level of system behaviour this agrees with round 1, where a loop without external signal neither sustained RSI content nor moved held-out behaviour. It is an analogy and not evidence for the mechanism: the write-ups measure a task score, never a representation, and none of their loops is closed on the model's output alone. What the pattern does expose is a gap in the experiment's own design: so far there is only the unanchored loop, so its decay has no anchored reference next to it, and the positive control of round 1 could not show that the pipeline registers a sustained loop.
patterns.what_to_do: For round 1b (design open), make an anchored loop the positive control. In each round mix a fraction a of a direction derived from a fixed, externally labelled statement set into the re-derived direction, and run a few values of a between 0 and 1. At a = 1 the direction is supplied afresh every round, so the RSI share must hold; this shows what a sustained loop looks like in the measurement, noise included. For values in between, the steady-state share is the quantity of interest; in a linear approximation it is a / (1 − (1 − a)·g) of the anchor's share, with g the unanchored gain per round, which gives a second estimate of g to set against the direct one from round 1. The counterpart in the toy self-training loop of (B) is the share of fresh real data per generation (the variable that, as far as I recall, the literature on models trained on their own outputs treats as decisive; this is not from the write-ups and should be checked before it is cited). If the frozen (B) plan lacks that axis, leave the plan as it is and run it as a separately labelled exploratory arm or defer it. Do not cite the write-ups as support for the round-1 mechanism.

patterns.pattern: A signal the model produces about its own output can be informative across items and carry nothing for choosing among its own outputs on one item.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: ARC2, analysis on 167 tasks: stated confidence tracks correctness across tasks ("There is clear correlation"; "the agent is more confident on tasks it is more likely to get right") but not within a task: "the agent is not more confident on correct passes than on incorrect passes"; "the lack of intra-task prediction makes this of limited value". Used to steer effort: "we weren't able to gain any score this way". It survives only as a tie-break in the selection rule. The link to the null result of the audit turn is the reader's inference; the authors do not draw it.
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Round 1 interpretation and the round-1b plan to separate what a state "reads as" from what later computation "uses". This is the nearest applied counterpart of the loop's read step, where the unpushed model reads the texts and a mean difference becomes the next direction. The confidence result is a behavioural case of a read-out that is real (it correlates) and tracks a coarse property of the item (in ARC: task difficulty) but not the property a loop would have to select on (in ARC: whether this attempt is right). Round 1's finding that the re-derived direction ends in a shared style direction has the same shape: the read step returns a coarse property of the texts. Analogy only; it suggests a test, it does not support a conclusion.
patterns.what_to_do: (1) Check on saved round-1 data, no GPU needed: are the pro and anti text sets entering each read step matched item by item (same prompts and seeds, equal counts, similar length)? If yes, the style direction is an effect of the push on the text and the round-1 reading stands. If no, recompute the round-1 directions on a matched subset before the attractor is interpreted, because a difference of unmatched means can contain differences in topic, length or register. (2) For round 1b, add a selection test, the direct counterpart of the confidence analysis: among several texts written for the same prompt, can the reader's projection on the RSI axis pick out the one written under the RSI push, above chance and better than the projection on the style direction? A loop needs this within-item information; a pooled correlation does not show it.

patterns.pattern: How far a model's own earlier output fixes what follows depends on the model: weak models lock in, the strong model barely does.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: Paper, for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: "continuations from winning and losing attempts' first responses won similarly often (49.8% vs 46.9%)"; no interval is given in the report. The authors use it to argue that the base policy is "strong, consistent". For smaller models they name "looping or refusing to drop an incorrect hypothesis" (paper) and "formatting mistakes, looping or sticking with an incorrect hypothesis" (author comment) as the failures RL removed; how often these occur is not reported for any model.
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Round 2 (B), the test of whether pushed content carries in context to a second turn. The write-ups measure an outcome (win or loss), not content, so this is an analogy. As a prior it points one way: the models that hold on to their own earlier text are the small ones, and Qwen3-1.7B is smaller than all of them. A positive second-turn carry could therefore be the generic tendency of a small model to continue the register and topic in its context, not something specific to RSI content. This is the same confound as the style attractor of round 1.
patterns.what_to_do: Two checks on the frozen (B) plan, without changing it. (1) Is second-turn carry also measured for a foreign axis pushed at matched damage? If not, report the round-2 result as carry of pushed content in general and put the foreign-axis comparison into round 1b. (2) Does the design draw several second-turn continuations per fixed first-turn text, as the write-up's comparison does? Without this, the effect of the first turn cannot be separated from sampling noise in the continuation.

patterns.pattern: The form in which the model's own history is fed back changes the result by several points, and the one self-closed step that helps uses the model's output as a carrier of state, not as a judge.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: At the context limit the model writes a summary and the context is reset to "the system prompt, original user prompt, summary, the last tool call, and a resume prompt". Replacing this with pruning the context to half costs "−4.7 ± 1.4" on ARC2 (paper: "Proper compaction (summarization instead of pruning) gains 4.7 ± 1.4 on ARC2"). Limits: not ablated on ARC3 ("due to code limitations"); compared with a cruder alternative only, not with a longer context; code and files persist next to the summary ("Files are not reset between levels"), so the summary is not the only carrier; nothing is reported on drift over successive summaries.
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Round 1b (loop closed in latent space versus through text) and the reading of round 1. The result shows that being closed through the model's own text is not by itself what makes a step useless; what the output is used for matters. For the experiment this is an analogy only: the summary carries task state under a task, the loop carries a pushed direction under no task. It fits treating the channel as something to measure: a write-then-read pass lets some axes through and not others (in round 1, style passes and RSI content decays).
patterns.what_to_do: Check that round 1b compares the two channels on one quantity: the gain of a single pass per axis (RSI axis, the style direction of round 1, a foreign axis) at matched damage, once through text and once in latent space. Optional and not from the write-ups: a neutral-rewrite control, in which the unpushed model rewrites the texts in a neutral register before the read step; if the fixed point of round 1 is style, it should weaken. Otherwise nothing: context only.

patterns.pattern: Training on generated text reproduces the surface of that text more readily than the competence behind it; weight updates helped only where an external reward met a specific, repairable failure, and more of it regressed.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: Own traces: "We fine-tuned Qwen's built-in MTP head on a combined dataset of ARC2 and ARC3 traces of our agents"; accepted tokens per draft rose "from 2.09 to 2.36" (ARC2) and "from 1.81 to 2.00" (ARC3). The head gets better at predicting what the model will write; the main model's answers do not change. Another model's text: "Distilling Kimi K3.1 Pro into Flash-Next. We found no benefit on ARC2; Kimi uses fewer tokens but does not improve score. The distilled Flash model also ends up more token efficient, but gets significantly more tasks wrong than the baseline Flash model." The student took over the teacher's brevity and lost accuracy; no numbers are given. Own rollouts with an external reward ("We directly optimized ARC score using policy-gradient methods"): gains on Qwen3.8-27B (ARC3 "3.02→11.9%" on training games, "9.40→22.1%" on 43 training-disjoint games), none on Flash-Next, and "longer single-game GRPO training regressed". Authors' reading: "smaller models exhibited clear failure modes, such as looping or refusing to drop an incorrect hypothesis, that RL could target"; "it seems likely that we can only steer it away from basic mistakes with task-specific training over increasing the capability ceiling". A commenter's hypothesis that such training "can at best pull pass@1 toward pass@k" is met with "That's broadly how we see it" but was not tested on Flash-Next. The write-ups contain no model trained on its own outputs without a reward, and no score-per-round curve.
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Round 2 (B) toy (a net trained on its own sampled outputs) and the reading of round 1. Analogy only, since no loop of that kind exists in the write-ups. Two ideas can be carried over as predictions to test, not as evidence. First, what survives a pass through generated text is the part that is easy to imitate (brevity, register), which has the same shape as the style attractor of round 1. Second, a loop that receives no new information can at most move probability mass the model already has. In the toy this is the difference between sharpening the existing distribution, which can look like a gain above 1 for some rounds and ends in collapse, and sustaining content.
patterns.what_to_do: For the toy in (B), check that the pre-set phase labels separate "sustain" from "sharpening that has not collapsed yet". That needs the trajectory over the whole pre-set horizon and several seeds, not a gain estimated from the first rounds, and the entropy or support size per generation recorded next to the tracked statistic, so that a gain above 1 with shrinking entropy is labelled as sharpening. If the frozen plan already does this: nothing. Do not present the distillation result as evidence for the style attractor; it is one sentence without numbers.

patterns.pattern: The write-ups hold almost nothing usable on temperature, and their sample-count result is weaker than it looks.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: Temperature was among the swept settings ("sampling settings such as temperature and reasoning effort"), but the reports contain no value and no per-value result; the one statement is "We tried using different sampling temperatures for reasoning, writing code, and summarizing, but found no benefit." Sample count: up to 2 instead of up to 10 independent passes changes the ARC2 score by "−0.2 ± 1.3", but "about 5% of tasks had finished no pass by the deadline, 32% one, 60% two and under 3% more than two", so the cap was binding for under 3% of tasks; this is a fact about the time budget, not about saturation. Diversity inside one pass did help: one answer instead of two costs "−3.2 ± 1.4" ("this is critical for puzzles with a small ambiguity the agents can't otherwise resolve"). Selection uses agreement between passes, with confidence as tie-break only (P5).
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Round 2 (B), the phase diagram in push size and temperature. No bearing on where the loop gain crosses 1, on the noise floor, or on the phases of the toy: there is no temperature value, no curve and no loop gain in the write-ups. One conceptual point carries over as an expectation, not as evidence: more samples help only when something selects among them. In the experiment's loop the step after sampling is a mean, which averages sampling variance out, so temperature should mainly move the noise floor unless it changes the kind of text that is written.
patterns.what_to_do: Nothing: context only. Do not cite the write-ups for temperature or for saturation with sample count. The one related check, equal numbers of texts per cell, is listed under P3.

patterns.pattern: "General beats domain-specific" means here that a stronger base model with a non-restrictive harness beats ARC-specific training and tricks. It is a claim about engineering strategy, conditional on model strength, and not about how "improving in general" is represented.
patterns.evidence_in_writeups: "The first untrained Qwen3.8-Flash-Next run scored 71.1%, 12.8 points above our best RL-trained Qwen3.8-27B (58.3%)." "Domain-specific post-training does not tackle this general reasoning capability, and so is not effective for capable base models." "general methods that leverage scale - in our case via the underlying model - ultimately beat methods that build in human domain knowledge." "We expect saturation of ARC3 will come from improved base models, not from any ARC-specific development." Qualifications in the write-ups: "getting some basic properties of the harness right does matter a lot" (Qwen Code without their task explanation: "17.8 points lower on ARC2 and 12.5 lower on ARC3 at matched generated tokens"); "Small gains still decide top ranks"; "Had Qwen3.6-27B remained the model of choice, these choices could have been correct." The comparison across models is not controlled, by the authors' own statement.
patterns.bearing_on_experiment: Round 2 (A). None as evidence. The shared word has two senses: the write-ups compare engineering strategies by task score; part (A) asks whether a concept composes with self-reference inside a representation. One observation is useful as context for the framing: every general gain in these write-ups came from outside the team's own loops ("switching to the recently released Qwen3.8-Flash-Next delivered a larger gain"), and the loops that fed outputs back into weights only repaired specific failures. The write-ups therefore contain no behavioural case of general improvement produced by a loop.
patterns.what_to_do: Nothing: context only. Do not cite the title claim in connection with part (A). If a later round needs a near-neighbour control axis for (A), "repairing specific errors" against "improving in general" is the distinction the authors draw themselves; that is an idea, not evidence.

not_relevant: Serving engineering (speculative decoding with the fine-tuned draft head, FP4 and INT4 quantisation, KV cache, ~900 and ~3200 tokens per second). The draft head trained on the agents' own traces looks like self-training, but the main model verifies every draft, so its outputs are unchanged; it is not a loop in which a model consumes its own outputs.

Expert pruning (512 to 307 experts with REAP, to 205 with distillation). Looks like the ablation and 'unlearning' of part (C). It is capacity removal chosen to leave task scores intact and says nothing about removing a direction or about damage-matched controls.

Agreement between independent passes as the selection rule ("ranked by how many passes returned them first, then by how many returned them second"). Looks like the convergence of independently started loops in round 1. The situation is the opposite: in ARC one right answer exists and wrong answers scatter, so agreement indicates correctness; in the loop, convergence from different starts marks the dominant direction of the write-and-read map, whatever its content.
'Up to 10 passes' against 'up to 2' (−0.2 ± 1.3). Looks like saturation with sample count; under 3% of tasks got more than two passes, so the cap was almost never binding.

Forced versus optional structure (mandatory check function −2.6 ± 1.4; mandatory world model −3.5 ± 2.0; "Tools should help the agent, not restrict it."). Looks like the damage done by a push applied at every position. It is a statement about restricting an agent's choices under a time budget and gives no information on KL damage or on norm-preserving pushes.

The code world model with automatic breadth-first search and the stop at the first mispredicted board. Looks related to predictive coding in the toys of part (C) because both involve a prediction error. One is a harness rule for an agent that writes programs, the other a learning rule; nothing transfers.

Images versus text for the grids (text only −6.2 ± 1.6; images plus text −2.6 ± 1.5). Looks like a 'the channel matters' result for the text-versus-latent comparison of round 1b. It concerns how the task is shown to the model, not what is carried between rounds.

'Telegraphic reasoning' triggered by "prompt injection". Looks like steering into a mode. It is a prompt-level effect on reasoning length; only its failure to transfer to the stronger model is used (P2).
RL algorithm details (PPO with a learned state critic, GRPO, DPPO). The experiment's loop has no reward, so nothing about these methods transfers.
"tiny recursive networks", cited as last year's paradigm. 'Recursive' there means iterated refinement inside one network, not recursive self-improvement.

"Our code is mostly LLM written" and supplements "mainly AI written with human review". Can be read as recursive self-improvement in practice; people directed and selected the work, and no loop was measured.

Scores and ranks as such (1st and 2nd place public, 87.36%, 70.24%, GPT-6 Astra 99.9%, GPT-6.1 54.8%) and a commenter's guess that the Qwen models were "hill climbed" on ARC. The first is context, the second speculation.
ARC-specific tools and prompt lines (segmentation, frame differences, the UNDO action, the efficiency sentence at +1.9 ± 1.6).
summary:
Verdict. The write-ups contain no evidence about residual-stream directions and can neither confirm nor refute the round-1 mechanism. They report task scores of agent systems, from one team, on models much larger than Qwen3-1.7B, mostly on the public leaderboard, with 95% intervals of about ±1.2 to ±2.1 points. The ARC2 and ARC3 texts largely coincide ("most content in both writeups is identical") and the paper summarises both, so this is one source, not three. I worked only from the three reader reports and used no tools; the readers did not see figures or supplements, and I cannot check the write-ups independently. I kept the readers' split between what is reported and what they inferred.

What bears on the experiment, by weight:

- Strong, and without analogy: the evaluation lesson (P1). The team ends with several results it cannot classify as null or under-measured, which is the position of round 1's positive control. Before the round-2 run: write down, from round-1 seed-to-seed spread, the smallest effect each gate and the positive control can detect; make "inconclusive" a pre-set outcome; confirm that the held-out statements did not inform round-2 design choices.

- Moderate: effects are conditional on the model, so a result on a 1.7B model cannot be extended to larger ones in either direction, and a failed recipe transfer does not show the feature is absent (P2). Comparisons need a matched quantity of text as well as matched damage (P3).

- Weak: at the level of behaviour the write-ups agree with round 1. Steps where the model only judges its own output show no measurable gain; measurable gains sit in components checked against execution or the environment. The contrast has exceptions (an external check that is null, a self-written summary that helps) and confounds (fixed time budget, low power, an agent that already has execution feedback). Its use is as a prompt for the open round-1b design: an anchored loop as positive control (P4), a within-item selection test of the read-out (P5), and a foreign-axis comparison for carry in context (P6).

- Analogy only: the form of the carrier, training on generated text, temperature and sample count, and the title claim (P7 to P10). The write-ups give no temperature values, no score-per-round curve, no model trained on its own outputs without a reward, and no measure of diversity or collapse, so the phase diagram of round 2 (B) has no applied counterpart here. "General" in the title is a different sense from part (A): it is about engineering strategy, not about a representation.

Rating rule: "strength" says how far the write-up evidence should change what the experiment does or concludes. Several to-dos are worth doing on their own merits although the evidence behind them is only an analogy; each entry says which is which. Nothing proposed changes the frozen round-2 plan: the items are checks on that plan, numbers to write down before the run, or inputs to round 1b. The one conditional exception is a fresh held-out set, needed only if the round-1 held-out statements informed round-2 design choices.

verdicts.reasoning:
Report. Every quote is in the reader reports. Three points are overstated or unverified. (1) The headline mixes two spreads: 'a few points' is the spread between single leaderboard submissions, while ±1.2 to ±2.1 are regression intervals from the offline sweeps. Against those intervals 11 of the 18 swept contrasts exclude zero (6 of 9 on ARC2, 5 of 9 on ARC3; three only just, and no correction for 18 comparisons is reported), and the large steps (model swap +12.8, text-only grids −6.2, pruning instead of summary −4.7) are clear of both spreads. What is true: seven contrasts cannot be told from zero, and no pair of single submissions could have resolved most effects. (2) 'As the write-ups' regression does' in to-do 5 is unverified: the reports do not say whether the OLS/LASSO model had interaction terms, and one reader even inferred one-at-a-time ablations against the other two reports. (3) Counter-evidence is left out: the ARC3 author comment that the configuration 'also generalized to our semi-private games', and a sweep set that contains 11 self-written games. 'Tuned on public tasks' is the ARC2 reader's inference. The 87.36/88.06 case shows only that one run was chosen; the team did not take the higher public score, so it shows no cost of choosing afterwards. The team's unclassifiable nulls come from low power and a design without 1:1 ablations, not from deciding after the data, so that lesson is not shown either.

Bridge. No analogy is needed, which is correct, but for the same reason the write-ups add no evidence: the point is general statistics, and the experiment's own failed positive control is the direct reason to act on it. By the claim's own rating rule (how far the write-up evidence should change what is done) this is weak, not strong.

Decision. To-dos 1 to 3 are the items most likely to change something and are worth doing before the run. They are not 'numbers only': if a gate cannot detect the expected effect, if the rules have only two outcomes, or if the held-out statements informed the design, the consequence is an amendment (more seeds or texts, a third outcome with a pre-set smallest effect of interest, a second held-out set). That is compatible with 'frozen before data' when it is dated and logged before any round-2 data exist, and it should be called an amendment. Three conditions the claim omits: compute the detectable effect from the round-1 variance only, never from the effect size round 1 observed, which only restates round 1's p-value; treat the round-1 spread as valid near the round-1 push size and temperature and as a lower bound elsewhere in the phase diagram; and if a new held-out set is made, keep the old one for continuity, since its round-1 result was a null and one design step after a null is a modest risk. On to-do 5: verdicts taken cell by cell multiply comparisons, so where the plan allows, read the boundary from the gain fitted as a surface over push size and temperature.
verdicts.corrected: Seven of the 18 swept contrasts have 95% intervals that include zero, single submissions of one configuration differ by 'a few points', and for the three ARC2 nulls and for RL on the strong model the authors say themselves that they cannot tell 'no effect' from too little resolving power. This illustrates a point that the experiment's own failed positive control already makes more directly; it is not additional evidence for it. Before the round-2 run, write down the smallest effect each gate and the positive control can detect (from round-1 variance, not from round-1 effect sizes) and make sure 'inconclusive' is a pre-set outcome. Where these checks bite they are dated pre-data amendments, not notes. Strength as write-up evidence: weak. Worth doing on its own merits: yes.

verdicts.reasoning:
Report. Quotes are accurate; the generalisation is not. (1) 'Almost every loop-related effect': only three things were tried on both a weaker and the stronger model. RL has numbers. The benefit of restrictive scaffolding on 27B is a statement with no 27B numbers in the reports. The concise-reasoning prompt has uncontrolled leaderboard numbers (~8 and ~10 points, against a submission spread of 'a few points') and is not a loop. The inference-time loop steps (audit, reflection, check function, compaction, passes) were ablated on Flash-Next alone. (2) The condition the authors name is not the model as such but how many repairable failures the baseline still makes, and the harness changes that as well: RL gains shrank on the same 27B model as the harness improved, harness changes alone took 27B from 3.02% to about 25% on the training games (RL: 11.9%), and the 27B ARC3 RL run 'used an earlier harness'. So the two models' training results also differ in harness version, a confound missing from the claim's list. (3) 'Changes size, generation': both models carry the version number 3.8 and Flash-Next's parameter count is not reported. What changes for certain is architecture, deployment form (pruned, quantised) and score. (4) 'The mode exists in Flash-Next': the authors report 'evidence of such a mode' and that they were 'unable to reliably trigger it', working on Flash-Next itself; whether the 27B prompt was reused unchanged is not stated. Strictly this is presence without a working handle inside one model, which maps better onto the round-1b question (what a state reads as versus what can be driven) than onto the cross-model toy of (A).

Bridge. Loose analogy for (a); for (b) the ordinary limit of a one-model study. 'A failed transfer does not show absence' is logic and needs no write-up. The reports say nothing about how a loop gain over residual directions changes with model size. The guess that a small model carries more of its own text fixes no sign: the same reports would equally support 'a 1.7B model carries style and not content'.

Decision. None in round 2. To-do (a) asks for the wrong second number. A probe trained in the target shows that the feature can be read out, the 'reads as' side. The control for a failed transfer is the same recipe derived and applied natively in the target. Report three numbers per target: readable natively, movable natively, movable with the source recipe; in toys this is cheap. To-do (b) contradicts the pattern: 'the round-1 settings on a larger model' is itself a recipe carried across models. Block, push size and axis must be re-derived, damage re-matched and a positive control run in the new model. That is a small study, not one number, and without it the number cannot be read.
verdicts.corrected: Three things tried on both a weaker and the stronger model did not carry over: RL gains (numbers), the benefit of restrictive scaffolding (statement only) and the prompt that triggers concise reasoning (uncontrolled leaderboard numbers). The authors tie this to how many repairable failures the baseline makes, which the harness changes as well as the model, and the two models' training results come from different harness versions. Inference-time loop steps were measured on one model only. For the experiment this is a general caution on scope and on how a failed transfer is read; it gives no information on the direction of any dependence on model size. Strength: weak.

verdicts.reasoning:
Report. Quotes are accurate, with two corrections. The +18.0 step is from the leaderboard chart whose caption says its steps 'are not controlled comparisons', so 'came from speed alone' is the authors' attribution of one uncontrolled step. And the authors' main convention is the opposite of matching: features are compared at fixed wall-clock time with token counts left free, precisely so that cost is charged; only the comparison with Qwen Code is at matched tokens.

Bridge. 'Needs no analogy' is not right. In the write-ups the quantity is a resource the system spends to reach a score. In the experiment the number of texts and tokens is the sample size of an estimator. The shared principle (hold the nuisance variable fixed) is generic, and picking out the nuisance variable in the loop owes nothing to the write-ups. So: a loose analogy that happens to point at sound statistics.

Decision. Here the check can change a result, and for a stronger reason than the claim gives. A share defined as a cosine or as a fraction of the norm is not just noisier when the mean difference is noisy; it is pulled toward its chance level, because noise lengthens the vector in directions unrelated to the axis. (A raw projection is not biased in this way.) Texts written at a higher temperature are typically more varied, so at equal counts a hotter cell reads a lower share even if the underlying map is the same, and that would shift the measured gain = 1 boundary. Equal counts do not remove this. A per-cell floor does only if it is estimated at that cell's own temperature and count; a split-half estimate (derive the direction on one half of the texts, measure the share on the other half) removes most of the bias directly. The frozen (B) plan already asks for a noise floor; what needs settling before the run is whether it is per cell. If it is, nothing changes.

One part of the to-do is not neutral: 'kept, or dropped with the count reported'. Dropping degenerate texts selects on an outcome of the push. The texts that survive are those the push changed least, which biases the re-derived direction toward zero in exactly the cells with large pushes. Keep all texts in the main analysis and filter only in a labelled sensitivity analysis. (The bias argument and the split-half suggestion are my reasoning, not content of the write-ups.)
verdicts.corrected: The write-ups score each change inside a fixed time budget, so their effects are net of cost, and the largest named leaderboard step (+18.0, uncontrolled) is attributed by the authors to a throughput change. By analogy only, this is a reminder to control the nuisance variable. In the loop that variable is the precision of the read step, not a resource: noise in the mean difference lowers a cosine-type share systematically, more so at higher temperature. Check that the (B) noise floor is estimated per cell at that cell's count and temperature, or use a split-half estimate, and keep all texts in the main analysis. Strength as write-up evidence: none to weak. Worth doing on its own merits: yes.

verdicts.reasoning:
Report. Numbers are quoted correctly and the claim lists most confounds itself. After checking the tables, less remains than the headline says.
The first half holds: audit turn, level reflection and strategy audit are all within ±1.4 to ±1.6 of zero. One confound is missing: the strategy audit fires only after 300,000 tokens on one level, so its average effect is capped by how seldom it fires.
The second half does not hold. Of the components checked against something external, two are null (check function, verified frame descriptions) and one is borderline (world model, +2.7 ± 2.1, with a test whose strictness the agent sets itself: 'the agent can configure its strictness'). The REPL case is not a test of anchoring: that harness still plays the game one action at a time, so it still gets a new frame after every action and both arms have the environment signal; what it lacks is computation and batching. The reports add that GPT-6.1 reached 54.8% in that restricted harness. Meanwhile most gains whose intervals exclude zero involve no external check: images (+6.2, +2.7), summary compaction (+4.7), two grids per pass (+3.2), the efficiency sentence (+1.9), and the task description (17.8 and 12.5 points). In these tables, being externally checked does not predict whether a component helps, and no arm anywhere lacks the external signal.

Bridge. The stated agreement with round 1 rests on two slips. First, the ARC nulls say that self-review did not raise a score; round 1 says that a content axis did not persist. A null audit is compatible with the answer mostly surviving its own re-reading, which would be persistence (the reports do not say how often the audit changed an answer). Second, the external signal in ARC is error feedback; in the proposed anchored loop it is re-injection of a direction, a source term. A driven system holds its level trivially, and that says nothing about feedback.

Decision. None for round 2. The round-1b proposal does not follow from the write-ups and has three weaknesses of its own. (1) At a = 1 there is no loop: the re-derived direction is discarded every round, so the rounds are repeats of the first pass. That gives the noise of a single pass, which is useful, but not 'what a sustained loop looks like'. (2) The formula a / (1 − (1 − a)·g) is correct for the unnormalised amplitude along one axis under a linear map without cross-talk. If the direction is rescaled to a set push size each round, which a push-size axis suggests, the steady share also depends on the gain of the competing directions (the style direction), and the formula no longer returns g. (3) The gap is narrower than stated: round 1 already registered a direction the loop sustains, the shared style direction. A positive control that uses the real loop is to start it on that direction, or on an easy foreign axis such as language or formality, and require the share to hold. The mixing design is better described as an injection-and-recovery calibration of the measurement. From memory and unverified: the literature on models trained on their own outputs does treat the share of fresh real data per generation as a central variable, together with whether generated data replace or accumulate next to the real data.
verdicts.corrected: Three self-review steps (ARC2 audit turn, ARC3 level reflection, ARC3 strategy audit) show no effect outside ±1.4 to ±1.6 points on a strong model that already has execution and environment feedback; the last of them fires rarely by design. No contrast with externally checked components can be drawn: two of those are null, one is borderline, the REPL comparison keeps the environment signal in both arms, and most resolved gains involve no external check. The nulls concern improvement of a task score, not persistence of content, so they neither agree nor disagree with round 1. Strength: none.

verdicts.reasoning:
Report. Accurate, and the link to the audit null is correctly marked as the reader's. 'Carry nothing' should read 'no detectable relation': the reports give no numbers, no interval and no count of tasks that have both a correct and an incorrect pass, and the selection rule still uses confidence within a task as a tie-break. The failure to steer effort is explained by the authors with cost ('those also tend to cost more tokens'), which concerns an across-task use, not the missing within-task signal.

Bridge. This is where it fails. 'A loop needs this within-item information' is true for a loop that improves by selecting among its own outputs, as in ARC. The experiment's loop does not select; it averages. It needs the average effect of the push within a prompt to be non-zero along the axis, which a matched design measures directly. It does not need a single text to be identifiable as pushed: with enough texts, a shift far too small for per-text identification still gives a well-defined gain. P9 of the same claim says this ('the step after sampling is a mean'), so P5 and P9 contradict each other and P9 is right. The proposed selection test measures per-text signal-to-noise, that is how many texts are needed. No decision depends on it.

Decision. To-do 1 (matched pro and anti sets) is sound, cheap and independent of the write-ups. But 'if yes, the round-1 reading stands' is too quick, because matching by prompt does not separate two readings of the shared attractor: (i) it is the dominant direction of the write-and-read map; (ii) it is an offset, a component that any push produces whatever its direction (for example the generic change in text under perturbation), which shows up if the contrast is pushed against unpushed and cancels if it is +d against -d. A constant offset also makes loops from different starts converge on one direction. Saved round-1 data can separate them: under (i) loops started at d and at -d end with opposite signs and unrelated starts end with mixed signs; under (ii) every start ends at the same signed direction. If round 1 compared end points by absolute or squared cosine, look at the signs; if no sign-flipped start exists, one is cheap to add. This matters for round 2, because under (ii) part of every gain measured in the (B) phase diagram is the offset. The sign test is my suggestion, not content of the write-ups.
verdicts.corrected: On 167 ARC2 tasks stated confidence tracks correctness across tasks and, by the authors' statement without numbers, not within a task. As a loose analogy this recalls that a pooled difference can carry structure between items. The experiment's loop averages and does not select, so it needs a mean shift within prompts, not identification of single texts; the selection test is not a requirement of the loop. Keep the matching check on saved round-1 data and add a sign test of the attractor (starts at d and at -d) to separate a dominant direction of the map from a push-independent offset. Strength as write-up evidence: none to weak.

verdicts.reasoning:
Report. The 49.8% vs 46.9% figure is quoted correctly, without interval or sample size. It does not measure lock-in. It says that which first response an attempt continued from made little difference to its win rate, and the authors use it for 'strong, consistent base policy': first responses are alike in quality. If they are alike, the number cannot show whether a continuation is bound by its first response. 'A direct measurement of path dependence' is the paper reader's inference. For weaker models there is no such number, only named failure modes without frequencies and the comment that Flash-Next 'made fewer of those obvious mistakes' (and that a better harness reduced them on 27B as well). A model difference in hypothesis fixation is asserted by the authors; 'weak models lock in, the strong model barely does' as a measured contrast is not in the reports.

Bridge. Loose, and it joins two different things. 'Refusing to drop an incorrect hypothesis' is failure to revise a belief against contrary evidence in a multi-turn agent run. Second-turn carry in (B) is in-context continuation of register and content, which every language model does, strong ones included. The prior 'smaller model, more carry' does not follow, and 9B and 27B against a Flash-Next of unreported size give no line to extrapolate to 1.7B.

Decision. To-do 1 (second-turn carry also for a foreign axis at matched damage) is a valid specificity control on general grounds and decides how a positive (B) result may be worded; if the frozen plan lacks it, wording the result as carry of pushed content in general is right. To-do 2 overstates: several continuations per first-turn text are not needed to identify the mean effect of the push, which a pushed-against-unpushed comparison over many first-turn texts gives. Replicates add precision and a split of the variance; no decision depends on them unless the planned number of first-turn texts is small.
verdicts.corrected: For the strong model, which first response an attempt continued from made little difference to its win rate (49.8% vs 46.9%, no interval); the authors read this as a consistent policy. For weaker models they name looping and hypothesis fixation without frequencies, and say the strong model and a better harness show fewer of them. No like-for-like measurement across models exists, and belief fixation in an agent run is not the same thing as in-context continuation. No prior for the 1.7B model follows. The foreign-axis control for second-turn carry stands on general grounds. Strength: none.

verdicts.reasoning:
Report. Accurate: the summary against pruning to half is −4.7 ± 1.4 on ARC2, and the limits are stated (ARC2 only, a cruder alternative only, no data on drift over successive summaries). One imprecision: the quote 'Files are not reset between levels' is from ARC3 while the number is from ARC2; that the workspace survives a compaction on ARC2 is the reader's inference. 'Helps' means 'beats pruning', not 'beats having no such step'.

Bridge. Rated as analogy only, correctly. The summary works under a task, with the task prompt shown again and state held in the workspace; the loop carries a pushed direction under no task.

Decision. None. The gain of a single pass per axis, once through text and once in latent space, is a sensible core measurement for round 1b, but it is not derived from the write-ups. On the optional neutral-rewrite control: the rewrite is itself one more write-and-read pass through the same model, so it would attenuate every axis by the channel's transfer and add the model's default register. A weaker fixed point afterwards would not show that the fixed point is style. I would not run it in that form.

Report. Quotes are accurate; they do not carry the generalisations.
'Reproduces the surface more readily than the competence behind it' rests on the Kimi distillation alone, and the same passage says 'Kimi uses fewer tokens but does not improve score'. The teacher had no score advantage, so there was no competence to pass on; the student took over the one thing that set the teacher apart, brevity, and paid in accuracy. The draft head says nothing on the point, since predicting the model's tokens is its whole job. The reports also hold a possible counterexample that the claim files under not relevant: pruning from 307 to 205 experts 'with distillation' and fine-tuning 'to preserve performance' (the training data and a before-and-after score are not reported).
'Helped only where an external reward met a repairable failure' is true of the score: RL on 27B is the only weight update with a held-out gain. The explanation is the authors' reading; no failure frequencies are given. 'More of it regressed' is one case, longer single-game GRPO on Flash-Next, which looks like fitting one game.
The idea that such training 'can at best pull pass@1 toward pass@k' is quoted one-sidedly. The same author comment reports 'cases where the trained model's pass@1 exceeded the base model's measured pass@k, including for 27B'.

Bridge. None, as the claim says. The two 'predictions' are general expectations about loops that receive no new information. They should be attributed to that reasoning and not to the write-ups.

Decision. The to-do for the (B) toy is useful on its own merits: record entropy or support size per generation over the full horizon and several seeds, so that a gain above 1 with shrinking entropy is not labelled 'sustain'. Logging these changes nothing in the plan; changing the phase labels does and needs a dated amendment. One addition of mine: in the simplest case, a categorical model refitted to N of its own samples at tau = 1, the loop is a neutral drift. The tracked statistic is constant in expectation and diversity is lost at a rate set by N. 'Sustain' is then a statement about sample size and horizon as much as about tau, so both should be fixed and reported with the phase labels.
verdicts.corrected: RL with the task score as reward raised held-out scores on the 27B model and not on Flash-Next; one longer single-game run on Flash-Next regressed. Distilling a teacher that used fewer tokens but scored no higher made the student more token-efficient and less accurate. Two fine-tunes on the system's own outputs did what they were for (draft head, pruning with distillation). None of this is a model trained in a loop on its own outputs, and none of it shows surface being copied before competence. Strength: none.

verdicts.reasoning:
Report. Accurate. The reading of the pass cap is better than the ARC2 reader's own ('saturated'): with under 3% of tasks getting more than two passes, −0.2 ± 1.3 says nothing about saturation. 'Diversity inside one pass' is a generous label for the two-grids result; the authors' explanation is that it matches the task, which allows two attempts.

Bridge. None claimed, correctly. One sentence in the bearing should be struck: 'temperature should mainly move the noise floor'. To first order the change a push makes to the next-token probabilities is the logit shift divided by the temperature, and near greedy decoding it becomes a threshold (nothing changes until the top token flips). Temperature therefore changes the average effect of the push on the text, that is the gain of the write step, and not only the scatter. Left in, the sentence invites reading a temperature dependence of the gain in (B) as a noise artefact. The other remark, 'more samples help only when something selects among them', is right for a loop that averages, and it contradicts the premise of P5.

Decision. None.

Report. Quotes are accurate. It is correct that 'general' has two unrelated senses here and that the comparison across models is uncontrolled.

Bridge. None claimed, correctly. Two caveats on the side remark that 'every general gain came from outside the team's own loops'. The harness and serving gains (about 17 points on ARC2 after the model swap; 18.8% to 70.2% on ARC3) came from the team's own score-driven tuning, which is a loop with an external signal and people in it. And the failures RL repaired (formatting, looping, hypothesis fixation) are not specific to ARC, so 'specific training repaired specific errors' blurs what the authors say. The remark that the write-ups contain no behavioural case of general improvement produced by a loop stands as the absence of a case, not as evidence against one.

Decision. None.

missed: Same restricted harness, two models (ARC3 report and paper): Flash-Next scores 0.17% with 'one action per call and no Python tool', while GPT-6.1 reaches 54.8% in 'the very limited ARC Prize adaptation' and was stopped for cost while still rising. Two consequences. That harness still plays the game one action at a time, so it is not an arm without external signal and cannot support P4. And it is the largest model-conditional contrast in the reports, running the other way from RL (absent on the weaker model, present on the stronger), which is what P2's 'in either direction' needs. Caveat: another model family and an unfinished run.

Author comment (ARC3 report): 'we saw cases where the trained model's pass@1 exceeded the base model's measured pass@k, including for 27B'. P8 and P10 cite only the commenter's idea that such training 'can at best pull pass@1 toward pass@k' and the reply 'That's broadly how we see it'. With a reward, training went beyond what the base model's samples contained. That is consistent with information entering through the reward and says nothing about a loop without one, but it means the pass@1-toward-pass@k idea is not a reported finding.

An effect size belongs to its baseline. RL gains shrank on the same 27B model as the harness improved; harness changes alone took 27B from 3.02% to about 25% on the training games against 11.9% from RL; the 27B ARC3 RL run 'used an earlier harness' and is not comparable with later numbers. For the experiment: when round 1b changes the pipeline (norm-preserving push, lens-based reading), differences from round 1 cannot be attributed unless one condition reproduces the round-1 setting inside the new pipeline. Check that the (B) grid contains the round-1 push size and temperature as one cell, and plan one such bridging condition for round 1b.

The only reported evidence on fitting to the public set points against it: 'It also generalized to our semi-private games, so we didn't see obvious signs of overfitting to the public ones' (ARC3 author comment), and the ARC3 sweep set mixes 21 official games with 11 self-written ones 'calibrated to approximate the semi-private test set'. P1 states 'tuned on public tasks' without this. It is also a working example of what P1's to-do 3 asks for: a second held-out set built by the team and not used for tuning.

The team's offline sweeps are a proxy for the target (a simulated Kaggle run on other hardware, a task mix chosen to match, expected baselines stated as ~67.5 and ~89) and were calibrated against it. The toys of round 2 stand in for the Qwen loop in the same way. By analogy of method: before a toy phase diagram is read across, check whether the toy reproduces what round 1 already established at the corresponding setting (decay of the injected content, different starts ending on one shared direction). If the frozen plan has no such step, record that the toy results carry no weight for the Qwen verdicts.

Trigger frequency. The strategy audit fires only after 300,000 tokens on one level, the world model is used 'on about half of the games', and more than two passes happen on under 3% of tasks. An average effect is frequency times effect when fired; the claim applies this to the pass cap only. For the experiment: next to any quantity averaged over all texts or held-out statements, report how the damage measure is spread across prompts (how many prompts the push barely touches), as a description and not as a filter. A null on the average can hide an effect confined to the prompts where the push acts.

The checker of the one externally checked component with a gain is set by the party it checks: test_world_model() 'is flexible, and the agent can configure its strictness'. This weakens P4's categories further. It has no bearing beyond confirming the experiment's practice of fixing thresholds outside the loop and before the data.

The same perturbation did different damage on different tasks: the INT4 KV cache was kept for ARC3 and rejected for ARC2 ('we found the drop in quality too high for ARC2'), while FP4 weights showed 'no noticeable degradation'. Analogy only, for the damage-matched controls of (C): controls matched on one scalar (KL) need not be matched in their damage to the quantity being read. Reporting that quantity under the foreign-axis push next to the KL would show whether they are. Low weight.

The nearest structural counterpart to the experiment's read step, a second agent that reads what the first one wrote ('A separate reviewer agent that provides suggestions to the agent actually playing'), is listed under not tried, as is retrying from a checkpoint. The write-ups therefore contain no data on a reader that did not write the text, one more reason they cannot speak to the write-and-read split of the loop.

Reporting selects among runs: '33 submissions below 0.1% are not shown' on the ARC3 progress chart. Minor, but it supports keeping a log of every run of the experiment, failed and aborted ones included, alongside P1's to-do 4.
summary:
Quotes: I found no misquote against the three reader reports; one quote is attached to the wrong benchmark (P7 uses an ARC3 sentence to qualify an ARC2 number). The faults are in the generalisations and in the bridges to the experiment.

Verdicts: P7, P9 and P10 hold; each says the write-ups have no bearing, which is right. P1, P2, P3, P5 and P6 hold in weaker form. P4 and P8 are in the same group, but in each the headline half fails. The tables show no contrast between externally checked and self-judging components: two of four checked components are null, most resolved gains involve no check, and every arm keeps the environment signal. And 'surface before competence' rests on a teacher that scored no higher than the student.

Bridge: nowhere is the step from an agent harness to a loop over residual-stream directions more than an analogy. P1 and P3 need no step because they are general statistics, and for that reason the write-ups add no evidence to them. Rated by the claim's own rule, P1 is not strong and P2 and P3 are not moderate; all ten are weak or none as evidence. Two analogies contain a slip: 'self-review does not raise a score' is not 'content does not persist' (P4), and belief fixation in an agent run is not in-context continuation (P6).

Two inferences should be struck because they could mislead the experiment: P5's 'a loop needs within-item information' (the loop averages and does not select, as P9 says), and P9's 'temperature should mainly move the noise floor' (temperature scales the effect of a push on the text itself).

Checks that can change a decision, all cheap and none resting on the write-ups: (1) the smallest detectable effect per gate and for the positive control, from round-1 variance only; (2) 'inconclusive' as a pre-set outcome; (3) a noise floor per cell of the (B) phase diagram at that cell's count and temperature, with all texts kept, because noise pulls a cosine-type share down systematically; (4) on saved round-1 data, the signs of the attractor reached from different and from sign-flipped starts, to separate a dominant direction of the map from a push-independent offset; (5) the round-1 setting as one cell of the (B) grid. Where these bite they are plan amendments, legitimate if dated before any round-2 data exist; the claim's statement that nothing changes the frozen plan is too comfortable.

Limits: I used no tools and worked only from the reader reports, so the write-ups themselves are unchecked. Checks 3 and 4, the critique of the anchored-loop formula and the remark on the model-collapse literature are my own reasoning or memory, not content of the write-ups. I do not know how round 1 defined 'pro' and 'anti' or whether it rescales the direction each round; where a point depends on that, it is stated conditionally.
